Nkandla: The Final Judgment

By: Este de Klerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Thursday was a day that changed the face of democratic South Africa - a victory for the Constitution and the rule of law.

It also showed that nobody was above the law, even President Jacob Zuma.

An important aspect was that the court had made declaratory orders that both Zuma and the National Assembly were in breach of their constitutional obligations.
The court found it was duty-bound to rule on that.

In a watershed unanimous judgment of the Constitutional Court on Thursday, the court found that President Jacob Zuma had acted inconsistently with the Constitution when he failed to comply with the Public Protector's remedial action on the upgrades to his Nkandla homestead.
The court ruled that Zuma had to personally pay back the money for some of the upgrades, following a determination by the National Treasury.

The Constitutional Court also found that the National Assembly erred when it dismissed Public Protector Thuli Madonsela's report.

"The resolution by the National Assembly absolving the president from compliance with the Public Protector's remedial action is inconsistent with the Constitution, is invalid, and set aside," Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng read from his unanimous judgment.

Mogoeng said a draft order Zuma circulated eight days before the case was heard in the Constitutional Court showed he accepted that the Public Protector's remedial action was binding.

Mogoeng said the president was enjoined to take definite steps to determine how much Zuma should pay for the swimming pool, cattle kraal, chicken run, visitors' centre, and amphitheatre built at Nkandla.

"The president failed to uphold, defend, and respect the Constitution," he said.

Only a court of law could have set aside the Public Protector's findings and remedial action.









Further information:
The Constitutional Court on Thursday handed down a precedent-setting judgment that both President Jacob Zuma and the National Assembly were in breach of their constitutional obligations in the Nkandla matter.

The court had thrown down the gauntlet to the ANC and it was no longer just about Zuma paying back the money.
The party would have to look at Zuma’s office going forward and whether they wanted him as head of state through local government elections, towards the elective conference next year, and into the 2019 national elections.

Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng read out the 53-page unanimous judgment on the applications lodged by the EFF and the DA.

Eleven orders were made:

- The court has exclusive jurisdiction to hear the application by the EFF

The EFF approached the court in a bid to have Zuma comply with Public Protector Thuli Madonsela’s remedial action that he repay the money spent on those Nkandla upgrades not needed for his security.

Mogoeng said conditions for the exercise of the court’s exclusive jurisdiction had been met.

"I conclude that the EFF has made out a case that the president’s alleged failure to comply with the remedial action, coupled with the failure to uphold the Constitution, relate to constitutional obligations imposed specifically on him," he said.

The Constitutional Court, as the highest court in the land, also had exclusive jurisdiction as it related to the National Assembly.

- The DA's application for direct access is granted

Mogoeng allowed the DA's application for access because it was similar to the EFF’s. The issues involved were extremely sensitive and of “high political importance”.

- The public protector’s findings against Zuma are binding in terms of the Constitution

Mogoeng said it was unlikely that those the public protector investigated would welcome unpleasant findings or "biting" remedial action.

"If compliance with remedial action taken were optional, then very few culprits, if any at all, would allow it to have any effect. And if it were, by design, never to have a binding effect, then it is incomprehensible just how the public protector could ever be effective in what she does and be able to contribute to the strengthening of our constitutional democracy."

He said the National Assembly was entitled to inquire into the correctness of the public protector’s findings and remedial action before it could hold the president accountable, but not in a way which undermined or trumped her mandate.

Mogoeng said the correct route would have been to challenge the Public Protector's report in court.

- Zuma’s failure to comply with the public protector’s remedial action is inconsistent with the Constitution and invalid

Zuma failed in his obligations to uphold, defend and respect the Constitution as the supreme law of the land. He failed in his duty to help and protect the public protector’s office to ensure its independence, impartiality, dignity and effectiveness.

- The National Assembly’s absolving Zuma from compliance with the public protector’s remedial action is invalid and set aside

"The National Assembly was duty-bound to hold the president accountable by facilitating and ensuring compliance with the decision of the public protector," Mogoeng said.

The National Assembly, like Zuma, could have genuinely believed that it was entitled to second-guess the remedial action.

"But, that still does not affect the unlawfulness of its preferred course of action."

- The president must reprimand the ministers involved

In a draft order submitted to the court before the hearing in February, Zuma said he was willing to reprimand ministers, in line with the public protector’s remedial action.

- Zuma must pay back the money (4 orders)

The Constitutional Court made four orders relating to the repayment of some of the R246m spent on non-security upgrades at Nkandla.

Firstly, National Treasury had to determine the reasonable cost of those features; namely the swimming pool, chicken run, cattle kraal, amphitheatre, and vistors’ centre.

Secondly, it had to determine how much of this amount Zuma should pay.

Treasury then had 60 days to report back to the court with its findings.

Finally, Zuma then had 45 days to pay back the money.

- Zuma, the National Assembly, and police minister had to pay the costs of the application, including the costs of two counsel.

Press Release:


Nkandla Judgement
The much-anticipated Constitutional Court ruling on controversial upgrades to President Jacob Zuma’s private Nkandla residence has been hailed as a seminal moment for South Africa’s democracy. Now, within 60 days, the National Treasury will determine how much of the state funds spent on his homestead President Zuma will have to personally pay back. Critically, the judgement reinforces the independence of the South African judiciary and the role of the Public Protector’s office. Carte Blanche asks: what lies ahead for Jacob Zuma?


Script:


NKANDLA: THE FINAL JUDGMENT SCRIPT
PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK
PRESIDENT JACOB ZUMA: The matter has caused a lot of frustration and confusion, for which I apologise, on my behalf and on behalf of government.
A President with “regret”… apologising to a nation he’d let down by breaking his oath of office.
JACOB ZUMA: I, Jacob Gedleyihlekisa Zuma, swear and will obey…
JUSTICE: MOGOENG MOGOENG: Observe…
JACOB ZUMA: Observe
JUSTICE: MOGOENG MOGOENG: Uphold…
JACOB ZUMA: Uphold
JUSTICE: MOGOENG MOGOENG: and maintain the Constitution
JACOB ZUMA: and maintain the Constitution…

JUSTICE: MOGOENG MOGOENG: …and all other law of the Republic.

JACOB ZUMA: …and all other law of the Republic.
Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng swore Jacob Zuma in to serve his second term as President.
JUSTICE MOGOENG MOGOENG: He is the first citizen of this country and occupies a position indispensable for the effective governance of our democratic country. Only upon him has the constitutional obligation to uphold, defend and respect the Constitution as the supreme law of the Republic been expressly imposed.
But in a scathing and very comprehensive judgment on Thursday, the very same judge who had sworn in President Zuma, ruled in the Constitutional Court that he had failed to uphold the Constitution by ignoring the Public Protector’s Nkandla report.
JUSTICE MOGOENG MOGOENG: The President’s failure to comply with the remedial action taken against him by the Public Protector is inconsistent with his obligations to uphold, defend and respect the Constitution as the supreme law of the Republic; The President thus failed to uphold, defend and respect the Constitution as the supreme law of the land.
PRESIDENT JACOB ZUMA: It all happened in good faith and there was no deliberate effort or intention to subvert the Constitution on my part.
President Zuma’s public address to the nation on Friday night, was the first time since 2014 that he’d called a live press conference from the Union Buildings.
While South Africans waited with bated breath, speculation was rife: was a possible resignation on the cards? The ANC’s top Six had been in lock-down for most of the day. But the President only responded to the judgment.
PRESIDENT JACOB ZUMA: I would like to emphasize that it was never my intention not to comply with the remedial action taken against me by the Public Protector or to irrespect her office.
DEREK LINK: After more than five years of hearings, disputes, investigations and reports, is this finally the end of Nkandlagate?
It all started in 2008 with some 27-million rand upgrades to then deputy-President Zuma’s homestead in Nkandla. When he became President the next year, government agreed to pick up the tab. But 27-million turned into a quarter of a billion.
Public Protector, Thuli Madonsela launched an investigation in 2012. Two years later, she released her report in which she found the President unduly benefitted from the security upgrades.
Zuma denied this all along.
ZUMA: My residence at Nkandla has been paid for by the Zuma family.
And after it’s own investigations, government concurred that Zuma didn’t have to pay back a cent – thus ignoring the Public Protector’s remedial actions.
MINISTER NATHI MNHLEKO: The State President is not liable to pay for any of the security feautures.
But this week’s judgment confirmed that the Public Protector’s rulings are binding.
JUSTICE MOGOENG MOGOENG: The remedial action that was taken against the President has a binding effect. This flows from the fact that the cattle kraal, chicken run, swimming pool, visitors’ centre and the amphitheatre were identified by the Public Protector as non-security features for which the President had to reimburse the State.
THULI MADONSELA: But in terms of the kind of findings, you know, very I would say very bold findings against the President, and also the findings against parliament, it was – they were true findings - but I didn't’ know if the constitutional court would go that far.
The Public Protector says the court has reaffirmed the supremacy of the Constitution.
THULI MADONSELA: Finally, the dream of the founders of our democracy, of giving them a gate where they can get justice without paying a cent, is going to be realized.
JUSTICE MOGOENG: The fathers and mothers of our Constitution, conceived of a way to give even to the poor and the marginalized, a voice and teeth that could bide corruption and abuse of state power and resources excruciatingly and that is the Public Protector. She is the embodiment of a biblical David, that the public is, who fights the most powerful and very well-resourced Goliath, that impropriety and corruption by government officials are.

PROF. MHOGO: If the president had not done what he failed to do we would not have had this judgment and we would have known what the powers of the public protector mean.

Constitutional Law expert at WITS University, professor Mtende Mhango, says rulings like these highlight the important role the judiciary plays.
PROF. MHOGO:. The founding fathers never have contemplated that a president would one day being asked to do something by public protector, he would refuse it and it would go to court and then we would know what they had in mind.
DEREK LINK: It was in February that the case brought against the President by the EFF and the DA was heard here in the Constitutional Court.

A dramatic U-turn came after five years of denial, when Zuma’s advocate said that his client accepted the Public Protector’s remedial action, which included paying back the money for the non-security upgrades.

ADVODATE GAUNTLETT: We accept it is not just a recommendation. She wanted certain things done. The undertaking is that those things should be done, because they must be done.

PRESIDENT JACOB ZUMA: I have consistently stated that I would pay an amount towards the Nkandla non-security upgrades.
But this turnaround by the President was deemed to be just an afterthought.
JULIUS MALEMA: When are you paying back the money?
PRESIDENT ZUMA: I have responded about the reports about Nkandla. The reports about Nkandla is not the Public Protector.
It was only when opposition parties took the matter to the Constitutional Court, that President Zuma finally changed his tune.
JULIUS MALEMA: That Constitutional Court judgment has got serious implications on Zuma’s holding of that office. How can you violate the Constitution and still think you can be entrusted with the responsibility of defending that Constitution. This book here – I doubt if he has read this book!
It wasn’t only Zuma’s dismissal of the Public Protector’s report that was critisized. The court ruled that the National Assembly was duty-bound to hold the President accountable.
THULI MADONSELA: I know that everyone is scathing on the president because of the original mistake but it is Parliament that stood until the last end and the issue was never about who has to tell who what to do. The issue was always about supporting and strengthening constitutional rights. It was always about in your own view, what’s right and what’s wrong.
JUSTICE MOGOENG MOGOENG: There was everything wrong with the National Assembly stepping into the shoes of the Public Protector, by passing a resolution that purported effectively to nullify the findings made and remedial action taken by the Public Protector and replacing them with its own findings and “remedial action”. This, The rule of law is dead against. It is another way of taking the law into one’s hands and thus constitutes self-help.
MOSIUOA LEKOTA: This judgment made a paramount point that the National Assembly also broke its own oath of office. You must understand the gravity of that statement, because we should not have been seen to support him breaking the Constitution. We wouldn’t go to Nkandla. We wouldn’t vote for this thing. We also now have broken our own oath of office.
The court ruled that if the President or National Assembly had wanted to challenge the Public Protector’s findings, they should have done so in court.
DEREK LINK: What commentators have been saying outside the Constitutional Court, is that whatever happens afterwards, today has been a watershed moment in the country’s democratic history.
BANTU HOLOMISA: The country has been a winner today and our democracy has been saved.
MOSIUOA LEKOTA: The Constitution reigns supreme here.
MMUSI MAIMANE: We are completely vindicated. It says that the future of south Africa is safe if we accept the fact that no leader is above any law.
STEPHEN GROOTTES: It’s saying that the constition is what matters, not how many seats you have in parliament. You still have to follow the law.
PRESIDENT ZUMA: I wish to reiterate that any action that has been found not to be in keeping with the Constitution happened because of a different approach and different legal advice.
JULIUS MALEMA: A wrong legal advise and also not knowing the law cannot be an excuse for not implementing your Constitutional obligations.
PROF. MHAGO: We have never had a case of this nature before in South Africa where the president was asked to do something that the constitution expects him to do and that he ignored – granted, and I think we have to keep in mind that at the time, the law was uncertain. There had never been a ruling, except for a ruling from the Western Cape High Court, that said that the public protector remedial action was not binding.
The DA has already tabled a fresh motion calling for Zuma to be impeached in terms of section 89 of the Constitution. This provides for the removal of a president on grounds that include a serious violation of the Constitution or the Law. The party also called for the resignation of Speaker Baleka Mbethe.
MMUSI MAIMANE: We can’t in South Africa have a party that gets co-opted into a grand scheming to defrauds South Africans or millions of rands, but then furthermore fails to defend our constitution. So it is a key platform for us to stand up and say Zuma must go!
STEPHEN GROOTTES: I think Nkandla is not quite finished yet. You’ve got Parliament itself, the National Assembly, will there be an impeachment proceeding? There probably will be something, but how it plays out and then how it plays out in Luthuli House.
PROF. MTENDE MHANGO: If the President is impeached – the legal implication is – there are two legal implications: one, he loses benefits so he can’t get a pension. He loses all benefits that he would have had if he leaves office. And secondly, he may never hold public office. So, it has massive implications and that is also why it requires a two thirds majority.
On Friday night at an ANC press conference, secretary general Gwede Mantashe accused opposition parties of wanting to tear the ruling party apart by calling for Zuma to be impeached.
GWEDE MANTASHE: The call for impeachment is nothing new nor is it genuine. It is an ongoing election platform ploy resuscitated every single year by the opposition in the form of either a vote of no confidence and now impeachment call.
On Friday, the National Treasury announced a task team was set up to determine how much the President will have to pay back.

STEPHEN GROOTTES: STEPHEN GROOTTES: It’s very interesting what’s going on in the ANC at the moment. Already there is a little bit of a pushback to a faction around President Jacob Zuma and sort-of the Gupta family and the people aligned with them. So, one way of looking at it is that it is likely to strengthen the hand of Gwede Mantashe as the Secretary General, it almost certainly strengthen the hand of Pravin Ghordan, the Finance Minister - he is under investigation by the Hawks, they seem to be controlled by President Jacob Zuma. Now the person who decides how much money Zuma has to pay back is Pravin Ghordan.

Parliament is set for a fiery start to its second term next week, when President Zuma will have to face the opposition parties who want him out.

PRESIDENT ZUMA: With hindsight, there are many matters that could have been handled differently, and which should never have been allowed to drag on this long, which we deeply regret.



PROMO’S

PROMO 1: 15”
DEREK LINK: CLIP 84: END: The Constitutional Court has ruled, but the question remains: how safe is President Zuma’s position at the Union Buildings?

PRESIDENT ZUMA: With hindsight, there are many matters that could have been handled differently



PROMO 2:15”

A watershed judgment in the country’s democratic history.

JUSTICE MOGOENG: The President thus failed to uphold, defend and respect the Constitution as the supreme law of the land.


PROMO 3: 10”

metadata.Summary: Thursday was a day that changed the face of democratic South Africa - a victory for the Constitution and the rule of law. It also showed that nobody was above the law, even President Jacob Zuma. An important aspect was that the court had made declaratory orders that both Zuma and the National Assembly were in breach of their constitutional obligations. The court found it was duty-bound to rule on that. In a watershed unanimous judgment of the Constitutional Court on Thursday, the court found that President Jacob Zuma had acted inconsistently with the Constitution when he failed to comply with the Public Protector's remedial action on the upgrades to his Nkandla homestead. The court ruled that Zuma had to personally pay back the money for some of the upgrades, following a determination by the National Treasury. The Constitutional Court also found that the National Assembly erred when it dismissed Public Protector Thuli Madonsela's report. "The resolution by the National Assembly absolving the president from compliance with the Public Protector's remedial action is inconsistent with the Constitution, is invalid, and set aside," Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng read from his unanimous judgment. Mogoeng said a draft order Zuma circulated eight days before the case was heard in the Constitutional Court showed he accepted that the Public Protector's remedial action was binding. Mogoeng said the president was enjoined to take definite steps to determine how much Zuma should pay for the swimming pool, cattle kraal, chicken run, visitors' centre, and amphitheatre built at Nkandla. "The president failed to uphold, defend, and respect the Constitution," he said. Only a court of law could have set aside the Public Protector's findings and remedial action.
metadata.Further information: The Constitutional Court on Thursday handed down a precedent-setting judgment that both President Jacob Zuma and the National Assembly were in breach of their constitutional obligations in the Nkandla matter. The court had thrown down the gauntlet to the ANC and it was no longer just about Zuma paying back the money. The party would have to look at Zuma’s office going forward and whether they wanted him as head of state through local government elections, towards the elective conference next year, and into the 2019 national elections. Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng read out the 53-page unanimous judgment on the applications lodged by the EFF and the DA. Eleven orders were made: - The court has exclusive jurisdiction to hear the application by the EFF The EFF approached the court in a bid to have Zuma comply with Public Protector Thuli Madonsela’s remedial action that he repay the money spent on those Nkandla upgrades not needed for his security. Mogoeng said conditions for the exercise of the court’s exclusive jurisdiction had been met. "I conclude that the EFF has made out a case that the president’s alleged failure to comply with the remedial action, coupled with the failure to uphold the Constitution, relate to constitutional obligations imposed specifically on him," he said. The Constitutional Court, as the highest court in the land, also had exclusive jurisdiction as it related to the National Assembly. - The DA's application for direct access is granted Mogoeng allowed the DA's application for access because it was similar to the EFF’s. The issues involved were extremely sensitive and of “high political importance”. - The public protector’s findings against Zuma are binding in terms of the Constitution Mogoeng said it was unlikely that those the public protector investigated would welcome unpleasant findings or "biting" remedial action. "If compliance with remedial action taken were optional, then very few culprits, if any at all, would allow it to have any effect. And if it were, by design, never to have a binding effect, then it is incomprehensible just how the public protector could ever be effective in what she does and be able to contribute to the strengthening of our constitutional democracy." He said the National Assembly was entitled to inquire into the correctness of the public protector’s findings and remedial action before it could hold the president accountable, but not in a way which undermined or trumped her mandate. Mogoeng said the correct route would have been to challenge the Public Protector's report in court. - Zuma’s failure to comply with the public protector’s remedial action is inconsistent with the Constitution and invalid Zuma failed in his obligations to uphold, defend and respect the Constitution as the supreme law of the land. He failed in his duty to help and protect the public protector’s office to ensure its independence, impartiality, dignity and effectiveness. - The National Assembly’s absolving Zuma from compliance with the public protector’s remedial action is invalid and set aside "The National Assembly was duty-bound to hold the president accountable by facilitating and ensuring compliance with the decision of the public protector," Mogoeng said. The National Assembly, like Zuma, could have genuinely believed that it was entitled to second-guess the remedial action. "But, that still does not affect the unlawfulness of its preferred course of action." - The president must reprimand the ministers involved In a draft order submitted to the court before the hearing in February, Zuma said he was willing to reprimand ministers, in line with the public protector’s remedial action. - Zuma must pay back the money (4 orders) The Constitutional Court made four orders relating to the repayment of some of the R246m spent on non-security upgrades at Nkandla. Firstly, National Treasury had to determine the reasonable cost of those features; namely the swimming pool, chicken run, cattle kraal, amphitheatre, and vistors’ centre. Secondly, it had to determine how much of this amount Zuma should pay. Treasury then had 60 days to report back to the court with its findings. Finally, Zuma then had 45 days to pay back the money. - Zuma, the National Assembly, and police minister had to pay the costs of the application, including the costs of two counsel.
